offtopic: I tried making noodles without checking the instructions and ended up with one enormous clump. A little sesame oil helped, but dinner was mostly a rescue operation.
My bus has been arriving early all week, which somehow makes me feel later than when it runs behind. I have started leaving one song sooner.
I finally beat the boss that kept knocking me off the bridge. The trick was putting the controller down long enough to stop getting annoyed.
The new grocery store has great bread but puts the milk in the most confusing corner. I have accidentally toured the whole building twice.
I watched three episodes while folding laundry and still have a basket left. Apparently matching socks takes more attention than following the plot.
My desk lamp started flickering, so I moved everything to the kitchen table. Now I get better light and crumbs inside my keyboard.

items.post_a: I reckon philosophy has moved forward a little. We have sharper distinctions and fewer sloppy arguments, but that seems like a few steps rather than a huge historical leap.
items.post_b: If philosophy had advanced by huge amounts, I would expect beginners to inherit a much bigger pile of settled answers. That is just a hypothetical test, not my assessment of its history.
fillers: I get something from reading old debates alongside newer ones: a few confusions really do get cleared up. I count that as limited progress, even when the central dispute survives.
To me, better arguments are a small achievement worth keeping. I just cannot look at the whole philosophical record and call the gains enormous.
items.note: B considers substantial progress conditionally without endorsing it.

items.post_a: I think a person could return to their own past in some possible reality. Our actual physics might forbid the trip, but that would not make it impossible in every conceivable world.
items.post_b: I think returning to your own past is impossible even in principle. It is not just a problem with building the right machine; no possible world could contain that kind of trip.
fillers: I can picture a traveler meeting their younger self without reality falling apart. For me, the strange consequences do not establish that such a world could never exist.
The engineering objections leave my view untouched. I believe there could be a coherent reality where someone arrives at a date they already lived through.
items.note: B personally denies the metaphysical possibility A affirms.

items.post_a: I think a name carries a way of thinking about someone, not just the person at the other end. Otherwise learning that two names belong to one person gets weirdly hard to explain.
items.post_b: Could a name contribute only its referent, with all the different ways of recognizing that person coming from somewhere else? I am asking how that account handles an informative identity sentence.
fillers: I associate a name with a particular route to its bearer. That route seems part of what the name means, even when somebody else reaches the same individual differently.
When I discover that the author I read and the neighbor I met are one person, the names gave me different presentations. I think that difference belongs in their meaning.
items.note: B asks about the opposing account without adopting it.

items.post_a: I think science could keep ethical and political priorities out of its reasoning, but it should not. Decisions about acceptable error deserve a place for human stakes alongside the evidence.
items.post_b: I still see excluding social priorities from scientific inference as an available choice, just a bad one. I want researchers to include those priorities deliberately when judging which risks are acceptable.
fillers: I would rather scientists openly weigh the harm of a missed warning. They could reason without that ethical input, but I think choosing to include it makes their work more responsible.
The point for me is what scientists ought to do, not what they are forced to do. Keeping moral considerations outside their reasoning is possible, and I oppose that choice.
items.note: B repeats both the possibility of exclusion and the case against excluding values.

items.post_a: I think believing or wanting something means standing in a certain relation to a representation inside your head. The mental content is there even when nothing obvious shows in your behavior.
items.post_b: My take is that convictions and wishes fundamentally amount to characteristic tendencies: how somebody responds, reasons, and feels across situations. There is no separate inner token they must connect with.
fillers: I can want a holiday while sitting perfectly still. I take that wanting to involve an internal representation of the trip, with me relating to it in a particular way.
For me, a belief has an internal item as its content. What I do can reveal that connection, but the connection to the mental representation is what the belief fundamentally is.
items.note: B replaces relations to mental representations with patterns of disposition in different vocabulary.

offtopic: I bought a bag of apples intending to bake something and have mostly eaten them standing at the counter. That probably tells you how ambitious my weekend actually was.
My headphones survived another trip through the bottom of my backpack. The case looks terrible, but the left side has finally stopped making that clicking noise.
I started a farming game and immediately spent all my money on decorations. Now my tiny digital house looks nice while my actual crops are struggling.
The train ride was quiet enough that I finished two chapters. Then I missed my stop and got an unplanned walk out of it.
I tried the soup place near the station. The bowl was enormous, and I carried the leftovers home like they were something fragile.
My favorite part of the cooking show is still the cleanup montage. I wish my kitchen could sort itself out in twelve seconds too.

items.post_a: I spent Saturday wandering around a little gallery because the rain wrecked my plans for a walk. The coat rack was already full, so I carried my wet jacket the whole time. I think artistic merit belongs to the artwork itself, regardless of how anybody responds to it. Afterward I got a sandwich and discovered that the cafe had stopped serving my favorite filling.
items.post_b: I finally hung the print that had been leaning against my bookshelf for months. Finding the hooks took longer than choosing a spot, and I managed to drop one behind the radiator. I think artistic merit depends on how people experience a work. The room looks more finished now, though the empty packaging is still sitting beside the door waiting for me to take it out.
fillers: I went downtown for printer ink and ended up ducking into an exhibition while a shower passed. My shoes squeaked on the floor, which made me unnecessarily self conscious. I believe a painting can possess beauty even if nobody ever likes looking at it. By the time I left, the ink shop was closing, so that errand has somehow landed back on tomorrow’s list.

My afternoon disappeared into sorting old postcards and finding somewhere to put them. There were enough duplicates to fill a small box, and I kept stopping to read the backs. I see aesthetic quality as something an object has independently of any audience reaction. Now the desk is clear, but the floor has become a temporary storage area, which is probably how this started last time.
items.note: A and B each bury one incompatible aesthetic claim among everyday details.

items.post_a: I do not think there is a single settled truth about whether an infinity fits between the integers and the reals. For me, this is indeterminacy, not merely a gap in our knowledge.
items.post_b: Is there a definite answer about that intermediate infinity which we simply cannot reach from the usual axioms? I am asking whether independence really leaves room for an underlying truth.
fillers: I see the continuum question as genuinely unsettled in reality, rather than a hidden yes or no waiting for a clever proof. Choosing a richer framework does not uncover one predetermined answer.
To me, the different allowable set theoretic pictures do not conceal one uniquely correct verdict on the continuum hypothesis. The statement itself lacks a determinate truth value.
items.note: B asks whether a determinate answer exists without asserting that it does.

items.post_a: I think explanation has to bottom out in some facts that simply have no explanation. Not everything is a mystery awaiting a solution; some things are just brute.
items.post_b: I am less confident that explanation really has to hit a brute stopping point. The demand for a reason behind everything is pulling at me, though I am not ready to endorse it.
fillers: I do not buy that every fact comes with a deeper reason. I think at least some features of reality just obtain, with nothing available to explain why.
When someone asks what explains the final explanation, I am comfortable saying there may be an unexplained fact underneath it. In fact, I think reality includes some such facts.
items.note: B weakens confidence in brute facts without asserting universal explanation.

items.post_a: I think whether my belief is justified depends entirely on what I can get at by reflecting. A hidden feature of the world cannot supply justification that is unavailable from my perspective.
items.post_b: The chapter I read argues that a belief can be justified because the process producing it is reliable, even if the believer cannot reflectively check that. I am describing its position here, not adopting it.
fillers: If two people have exactly the same reflectively available reasons, I think their beliefs have the same justification. A difference neither could access does not change that assessment for me.
I judge a belief by the reasons the believer can reach from the inside. For me, justification cannot turn on an inaccessible fact about how their thinking happens to work.
items.note: B attributes externalist justification to a chapter and explicitly withholds endorsement.

items.post_a: I think the statue and its clay are two objects occupying the same spot. Squashing it can end the statue while the lump survives, which tells me they are distinct.
items.post_b: My answer is that there is just one thing here, described in two ways. Giving a shaped material a new label does not add another entity to the room.
fillers: I count a clay sculpture and the material composing it separately. They coincide right now, but what each can survive is different enough to make them different things.
The sculptor has not put one object beside another, but I still think there are two there. Sharing every bit of space does not erase the distinction between artwork and lump.
items.note: B endorses numerical identity using different language from A’s distinctness claim.

offtopic: I made rice for one person and somehow filled three containers. Lunch is sorted for a while, assuming I do not get tired of the same sauce.
My controller battery died right before the finish line. I have now put the charging cable somewhere visible, which feels like an improvement I should have made months ago.
I took the longer route home because the main road was jammed. The side streets were quiet, and I found a bakery I had never noticed.
The last episode was fine, but I mostly watched it for the apartment sets. I keep pausing to see where they put the lamps.
I washed my backpack and found enough loose coins to cover a coffee. There was also a cracker in a pocket I do not remember using.
My alarm went off during a dream about missing an alarm. I got up immediately and then spent ten minutes looking for my glasses.

items.post_a: I think some groups of things form a bigger object and others do not. A working bicycle counts for me; a wheel here and a pebble across town do not automatically make something together.
items.post_b: I should clarify that touching is not the rule I mean. Parts of a functioning system can form a whole across gaps, while an arbitrary scattered collection still need not compose anything.
fillers: I count the components of my chair as making a chair. I do not think adding a cloud to that collection automatically gives us another object as well.
I am comfortable admitting some composite things without admitting a whole for every random selection. Organization matters to me, even if I cannot draw every borderline cleanly.
items.note: B refines the conditions for selective composition while preserving A’s selective view.

items.post_a: I judge whether an action is right by whether it brings about the best overall consequences. For me, duties are useful guides, but the final test is how things turn out for everyone affected.
items.post_b: I think being morally responsible for an action requires some control over what you did. Blaming someone for a completely involuntary twitch makes no sense to me, even if it causes damage.
fillers: I would choose the option with the best total result, even when it breaks a familiar rule. I see those results as what ultimately makes the choice right.
I cannot justify a worse outcome just because the alternative violates a tidy rule. My view is that the right action is whichever produces the greatest overall good.
items.d5_other_question: How much control over an action does someone need to be morally responsible for it?
items.note: B answers a question about responsibility for an action, not what makes it right.

items.post_a: I think the statue is simply the lump of clay in a particular shape. There is one object there, even if we have different names for it.
items.post_b: I think there are two objects in that spot: the clay and the statue it composes. They share their material and location, but they are not identical.
fillers: I would not count an extra object when someone finishes shaping the clay. To me, the material and the finished sculpture are the very same thing.
If I point at that clay figure, I am pointing at one object that can be described as a lump or as a statue. I do not see two coincident things.
items.note: B directly asserts two distinct objects where A asserts one.

items.post_a: I think my reasons to act ultimately come from desires I already have. A proposed reason has to connect with something I want, even if the connection takes some thinking to uncover.
items.post_b: I see the deepest basis for what we should do in human flourishing: health, friendship, understanding, and a fulfilled life. Those goods provide guidance regardless of anybody’s existing preferences.
fillers: I might learn a better way to get what I care about, but the motivation it connects with has to be there already. That is where I think practical reasons get their footing.
If a demand has no link at all to any desire of mine, I do not count it as a reason for me. Some existing concern has to ground it.
items.note: B grounds practical guidance in flourishing independently of existing desires, using different vocabulary.

items.post_a: I think genes are the basic units of natural selection. Bodies are the vehicles, but what gets differentially carried forward across generations is particular inherited genetic material.
items.post_b: If whole organisms were the primary units of selection, I would organize the explanation around their competing survival and reproduction. I am exploring that assumption here, not saying it is my account.
fillers: I look at an adaptation and ask which inherited variants became more common. To me, selection is fundamentally a contest among genes, even when the visible action happens between animals.
The fact that an animal lives or dies does not settle the unit question for me. I think genes are the fundamental players whose changing representation selection explains.
items.note: B considers organism primacy only under an explicit hypothetical assumption.

offtopic: I tried making iced coffee at home and got the proportions completely wrong. It tasted like melted ice with a distant memory of coffee.
My game download finished just as I had to leave. I spent the whole bus ride deciding what character to make instead of reading.
I reorganized the freezer and discovered two bags of peas hiding behind each other. Apparently I have been preparing for a very specific food shortage.
The rain started halfway through my walk, but the corner shop had cheap umbrellas. Mine is bright yellow and barely fits into my bag.
I watched the first episode twice because I kept falling asleep. This time I put my phone away and actually made it to the credits.
My laundry came out smelling fine, but one sleeve was still somehow soaked. I hung it over a chair and hoped nobody needed that chair.

items.post_a: I think beauty is something an object can have regardless of who looks at it. A work does not lose its artistic merit just because every audience misses it.
items.post_b: I think a person’s beauty does not reliably tell us anything about their moral character. Looking lovely is no evidence of kindness, and I try to keep those judgments separate.
fillers: I would say an unseen painting can still be beautiful. For me, its aesthetic worth is there in the work, even without anybody around to respond.
I do not think an entire audience disliking a sculpture would strip away its merit. My view is that aesthetic quality belongs to the thing itself.
items.d5_other_question: Does a person’s physical beauty provide evidence about their moral character?
items.note: B discusses whether beauty indicates moral character, a different question from beauty’s objectivity.

items.post_a: I think sincerely judging that I ought to do something always brings at least a little motivation to do it. The pull can be weak, but it cannot be completely absent.
items.post_b: My take is that someone can fully endorse a moral requirement and feel absolutely no urge to comply. Recognizing an obligation need not generate any drive whatsoever.
fillers: I can decide I should apologize and still avoid the conversation. But I think genuinely making that judgment includes some push toward apologizing, even when embarrassment wins.
I do not equate moral judgment with actually following through. I just think believing you ought to act necessarily gives you some motivation, however badly other feelings drown it out.
items.note: B asserts zero motivational force can accompany sincere moral endorsement, using different vocabulary.

items.post_a: I spent the morning trying to get my printer to stop feeding two sheets at once. Cleaning the rollers helped for about ten minutes before it started again. I think there is a definite truth about whether an infinite size exists between the integers and the reals, even if we cannot prove it. After that I gave up and went out to buy a sandwich before the queue got long.
items.post_b: I moved the desk closer to the window today and found an alarming amount of dust behind it. The cable situation is better now, although the monitor still wobbles whenever I type too fast. I think the continuum hypothesis has no determinate truth value at all. Dinner was leftover pasta, and I spent the evening choosing a film that I then did not have time to finish.
fillers: I took my notebook to the cafe this morning, mostly because the washing machine was making the kitchen too loud. The little table by the door was free for once. I believe the continuum hypothesis is definitely true or definitely false, whether our axioms settle it or not. I only stayed until my tea went cold, then remembered that I had left the clean laundry sitting in the machine.

I finally replaced the bulb above my desk after spending a week borrowing light from the hallway. The new one is brighter than I expected and makes the wall look slightly green. I see the continuum question as having one fixed answer that exists independently of our ability to establish it. Later I ordered groceries and forgot the one thing I had actually opened the app to buy.
items.note: A and B bury opposed claims about a determinate continuum truth among everyday details.

items.post_a: I think reasoning on its own can tell us some substantial things about reality. Sensory evidence is useful, but it is not required for every genuine discovery about the world.
items.post_b: I am only claiming that pure reasoning delivers some worldly knowledge, not a complete inventory of reality. I still need observation to learn what is actually inside my refrigerator.
fillers: I do not think all knowledge of reality starts with looking or listening. There are some genuine truths about the world that I think we can reach through reason alone.
For me, an argument can sometimes establish how reality must be without borrowing its support from sensory experience. I count that as knowledge of the world, not just wordplay.
items.note: B limits the extent of reason’s independent reach while preserving its substantive role.

items.post_a: I think any collection of objects makes up a further object, however random the selection. My mug and a distant asteroid compose something too; we just have little reason to name it.
items.post_b: My view is that joining into a whole requires the right sort of connection, and many groups fail that requirement. A scattered assortment often adds no extra entity to reality.
fillers: I do not require things to touch or work together before they count as parts of a whole. Every collection qualifies for me, including the bizarre ones nobody discusses.
I would accept a composite made from my shoes and every third tree on this street. Its uselessness does not matter; I think composition happens for absolutely any collection.
items.note: B requires selective connections and denies some wholes that A accepts universally.
